title: Arrangement Tricks
intro: Arranging is mostly moving big blocks of time around without breaking anything. These tricks let you restructure a whole song in seconds instead of dragging regions one by one and praying.

tips.t: Use the Arrangement track to move whole sections
tips.d: Open Global Tracks with G, enable the Arrangement track, and drop markers on your Verse, Chorus and Bridge. Now drag the Chorus marker and the entire section — every track, every automation point — moves with it.

tips.t: ⌘-drag one arrangement marker onto another to swap sections
tips.d: A plain drag moves or inserts. Hold ⌘ while dragging one marker onto another and they swap places. Trying three song orders takes about fifteen seconds.

tips.t: ⌥‑drag an arrangement marker to duplicate a section
tips.d: Hold ⌥ and drag any arrangement marker to copy that entire section, contents and all, to a new point in the timeline.

tips.t: Delete a section and close the gap
tips.d: Select the arrangement marker and press Delete once — that removes the section's regions. Press Delete again and the marker goes too, pulling everything after it back to close the hole.

tips.t: Insert silence across the whole project
tips.d: Set the locators, then Edit > Cut/Insert Time > Insert Silence at Locators. Every track and every automation point shifts. This is how you add two bars to an intro without wrecking the mix.

tips.t: Snap arrangement markers to your actual section boundaries
tips.d: Select a region that spans exactly one section, hit U to set the locators to it, then create the arrangement marker. It lands perfectly instead of approximately.

tips.t: Repeat regions numerically instead of dragging
tips.d: Select regions and hit ⌘R for a single repeat, or use Edit > Repeat Multiple… to type an exact number of copies and choose whether they land as copies or aliases.

tips.t: Loop a region instead of copying it
tips.d: Grab the top‑right corner of a region and drag right to loop it. Looped regions update everywhere when you edit the original, and they cost nothing to change.

tips.t: Convert loops to real regions only at the very end
tips.d: Edit > Convert > Loops to Regions, or control-click the region and choose Convert. Stay looped as long as possible so a single edit propagates, then commit when the arrangement is locked.

tips.t: Use aliases for parts that must stay identical
tips.d: ⌥⇧‑drag a MIDI region to create an alias. Edit the parent and every alias follows. Perfect for doubled parts across a whole song.

tips.t: Make a folder out of a section
tips.d: Select every region in a section and use Functions > Folder > Pack Folder. The arrangement collapses to one block you can move, copy and mute as a unit.
Open the colour palette with ⌥C and give every chorus the same colour across all tracks. You can then read the arrangement at a glance from fully zoomed out.

tips.t: Zoom all the way out and squint
tips.d: Hit Z with nothing selected to fit the whole project on screen. If the energy shape of the song is not visible from the region blocks alone, the arrangement is probably flat.

tips.t: Use Track Stacks to collapse instrument families
tips.d: Select related tracks and hit ⇧⌘D, then choose Summing Stack in the dialog. Drums become one lane and the arrangement becomes readable.

tips.t: Solo an arrangement section with the locators
tips.d: Click the arrangement marker to select that section's regions, hit U to set the locators to them, then C. Three keys and you are looping exactly that section.

tips.t: Mute regions instead of deleting them while experimenting
tips.d: Click a region with the Mute tool, or select and press M. Arrangement experiments become reversible without touching undo.

tips.t: Keep a “graveyard” track at the bottom
tips.d: Make one muted, hidden track and drag every rejected idea onto it. Nothing is ever deleted, and the good version of that rejected idea is there when you need it three weeks later.

tips.t: Use markers for notes to self, not just sections
tips.d: Create a marker from the Global Tracks marker lane, then rename it “fix snare here” or “vocal comp needed”. Your to‑do list lives on the timeline instead of on paper.
